title: Materials Design Principles

pts: One influential model starts materials design from a single, engaging authentic or semi-authentic text, deriving all activities from it.
This contrasts with a language-point-driven approach, where a grammar or vocabulary target comes first and text is chosen to fit it.
This connects to Unit 41's authentic-materials-at-scale principles, examined here as a formal design framework.

v: Teachers or trainee teachers in groups of four
One short engaging text per group

items: Give each group one short text likely to engage learners emotionally or intellectually, for example a poem, a short news story or a personal narrative.

Groups design a sequence from the text: a readiness activity, an initial experience of the text, a personal response, then activities that develop the response and finally attention to one language feature found in the text.
Groups then take the same language feature and design a second lesson starting from the feature, choosing or writing a text to fit it.
Compare the two lessons for engagement, practice of the feature and suitability for a class of 50.
Start from a home-language text and its English translation.
Support: provide the stage labels on a card for each group.
Challenge: write learner instructions for every stage, ready to use.

blocks.x: A text-driven sequence outline (written for this book), based on a short narrative about a girl in Hubballi who repairs bicycles:

lines: Readiness: Tell your partner, in any language, about something you fixed.
Experience: Listen as the teacher reads. Do not write.
Response: How did the girl feel at the end? How do you know?
Development: Write the story from the customer’s point of view.
Language discovery: Find all the verbs ending in -ed. What do they tell us about time?

blocks.x: Tomlinson describes this as a Text-Driven Approach: the text is chosen first for its potential to engage, and the language focus emerges from it (Tomlinson 2011) [VERIFY chapter and stage labels in Tomlinson’s text-driven framework]. In a language-point-driven approach the target comes first and texts are written to contain it, often at the cost of interest.

body: Purpose: to contrast two design routes. Content: two paths to a classroom, one starting from an open storybook, the other from a grammar label. Style: clean, warm. Board version: two arrows starting from ‘text’ and ‘language point’.

items: Google Docs (free) for sharing sequences across a training group.

blocks.x: Sequences written on chart paper and displayed for a gallery walk.

pts: Materials should expose learners to rich, meaningful input; engage them affectively and cognitively; and provide opportunities for meaningful output.
These principles draw directly on the SLA theories examined in Unit 77, applied specifically to material design decisions.
This gives materials writers a research-grounded checklist beyond pure intuition or convention.

v: A coursebook unit; a principles checklist

items: Prepare a short checklist of five principles: rich input, affective engagement, cognitive engagement, attention to form in meaningful use and opportunities for meaningful output.
Pairs choose one textbook unit and find evidence for each principle, activity by activity.
They rate each principle as ‘strong’, ‘some’ or ‘absent’ and note the evidence.
For the weakest principle, they design one small addition. Unit 77 provides the SLA background for each principle.
Use the checklist on a worksheet the pair wrote themselves (Unit 69).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A pair’s notes on a Class 8 unit (written for this book):

lines: Rich input: One reading text of 300 words. Some.
Affective engagement: The text is about a festival; no personal response task. Some.
Cognitive engagement: Questions are all factual recall. Absent.
Meaningful output: Fill in the blanks only. Absent.
Addition: Learners describe a festival from their own village to a partner.

blocks.x: These principles are drawn from Tomlinson’s (2011) synthesis. They are reasonable inferences from a large body of SLA research, not rules proved by experiment, and are best treated as questions.

body: Purpose: to summarize SLA-informed principles. Content: a hand holding a worksheet with five labelled magnifying glasses around it: input, feeling, thinking, form and output. Style: friendly. Board version: a rectangle with five labels.

items: Google Forms (free) to turn the checklist into a quick shared survey for a group of teachers.

body: Tomlinson (2012) notes that materials development began to be treated as an academic field only relatively recently; until then, most materials writers learned the craft by doing it, often without formal training in how languages are learned.

pts: What counts as 'authentic' material, and whether authenticity itself reliably improves learning outcomes, remains a genuinely debated research question.
This adds nuance to Unit 41's practical authenticity guidance — the research evidence for authenticity's benefits is more mixed than commonly assumed.
This doesn't invalidate authentic-materials use, but it does argue against treating authenticity as automatically, self-evidently superior.

items: Prepare six texts: a railway announcement, a textbook dialogue, a graded reader page, a WhatsApp message, a newspaper paragraph and a learner’s letter.
Groups place each text on a line from ‘not authentic’ to ‘authentic’ and justify each placement.
Introduce Widdowson’s distinction between a genuine text and an authentic response to it. Groups reconsider the line.
Discuss: when would a simplified text serve these learners better than a genuine one? Link to Unit 41.
Add texts in Indian and British English: whose English counts as authentic (Unit 74)?
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: A: The railway announcement is authentic. It was not written for learners.
B: But if our Class 6 learners understand nothing, what are they doing with it?
B: The textbook dialogue is not genuine, but if they adapt it to their own lives, their response is real.

blocks.x: Gilmore (2007) reviews the research and concludes that authentic materials can help, particularly for developing awareness of real language use, but that the evidence is mixed and depends on the learners, the text and the task. Authenticity is one consideration among several, not a guarantee of learning.

body: Purpose: to show authenticity as a continuum. Content: a rope across a training hall with text cards pegged along it; a teacher moves one card. Style: realistic, Indian training hall. Board version: a line with six small rectangles.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for groups to place and move text cards on a shared line.

blocks.x: Cards pegged on a string or taped along a wall.

pts: Research on task design examines which specific task features — information gap, task complexity, planning time — most reliably affect learning outcomes.
This grounds Unit 28's task-cycle guidance and Unit 29's trilogy framework in their underlying empirical research base.
This research field continues to actively develop, refining exactly which task features matter most and why.
points.who: Peter Skehan and Rod Ellis's task design research

v: A speaking task; a phone recorder or a tally sheet

items: Choose a speaking task you use regularly, such as describing a picture.
Run it as usual in one class. In a parallel class, change one feature only: add an information gap, allow two minutes’ planning or reduce the items to describe.
Record two or three pairs in each class, or tally features such as pauses, self-corrections and longer sentences.
Compare. Did the change affect fluency, accuracy or complexity? Unit 29 explains these three dimensions.
Run both versions in one class on different days, with different pictures of similar difficulty.
Not applicable (classroom research activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s notes (written for this book):

lines: Version A: Pairs describe the same market picture. Short answers; much Kannada; few full sentences.
Version B: Each partner has a different picture and must find five differences. Two minutes to plan. More questions in English; longer sentences; still some pauses.
Conclusion: The information gap created a reason to speak. Planning helped them try longer sentences.

blocks.x: Skehan (1998) and Ellis (2003) review research showing that task features such as planning time, information structure and task complexity can shift learner performance between fluency, accuracy and complexity. Effects vary across studies. One classroom comparison proves nothing general, but it gives useful local evidence.

body: Purpose: to show that task features can be varied systematically. Content: a mixing desk with three sliders labelled ‘information gap’, ‘complexity’ and ‘planning time’, and a pair of learners speaking beside it. Style: clear, slightly playful. Board version: three vertical lines with a slider on each.

items: A phone voice recorder; Audacity (free, open source) for replaying recordings.

blocks.x: A tally sheet with three columns: pauses, self-corrections, long sentences.

pts: Formal materials-evaluation checklists assess coursebooks and materials against explicit, research-grounded criteria, not just impression.
This connects directly to Unit 13's coursebook-audit guidance, offering a more systematic, formalised version of that practice.
Using an explicit framework produces more consistent, defensible evaluation than unstructured impression alone.

v: DIET faculty or textbook review committees
Two coursebook units; an evaluation framework

items: Each participant first gives two coursebook units a quick overall rating out of ten, without discussion.
Introduce a short framework with explicit criteria, for example learner needs, input quality, task quality, cultural relevance, home-language use and assessment.
Participants rate both units again against each criterion, citing evidence from the page.
Compare the spread of the two sets of ratings and discuss which could be defended to a committee. Unit 13 offers a simpler audit.
Adapt the criteria to a specific context, such as a Kannada-medium rural school or an urban English-medium school.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Ratings from a review group (written for this book):

lines: Impression ratings for Unit A: 4, 8, 6, 9, 5.
Criterion ratings for Unit A, task quality: 2, 2, 3, 2, 2 out of 5; evidence: ‘all tasks are gap-fill or copy’.
A: Our first scores were all over the place.
B: The criteria made us all look at the same things.

blocks.x: McGrath (2016) argues for explicit, context-sensitive criteria rather than impression. He also recommends evaluating in stages, from first-glance screening to close analysis and evaluation after use.

body: Purpose: to show structured evaluation. Content: a teacher puzzling over a coursebook, then the same teacher with a clipboard of criteria and ticks. Style: neat. Board version: a book with a question mark, then a book with a checklist.

items: Google Sheets (free) for collecting ratings from several reviewers and comparing them.

blocks.x: A printed evaluation grid with a column for evidence.

pts: Published materials sometimes lag behind current SLA research findings, reflecting commercial, institutional, and market constraints.
This is part of the rationale for Tier III's materials-writing skill (Unit 69) — self-written materials can more directly reflect current evidence.
Being aware of this gap supports more critical, informed use of published materials generally.

v: A recent coursebook; a short list of research-informed features

items: Give groups a list of features that research supports, for example recycling of vocabulary, meaningful speaking tasks, attention to form in context and use of home languages.
Groups check how far a current coursebook reflects each feature.
For each gap, groups suggest a reason, such as examination format, cost or the need to suit many contexts.
Groups decide how a teacher could fill one gap without rewriting the whole book. Unit 69 offers techniques.
Compare two editions of the same textbook.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A group’s summary (written for this book):

lines: Feature: Vocabulary recycled across units. Found: New words listed once; rarely seen again. Possible reason: Units written by different authors.
Feature: Home languages as a resource. Found: Absent. Possible reason: Book written for the whole state.
Teacher action: A five-minute weekly word review from earlier units.

blocks.x: Reviews of published courses have noted that some widely used materials do not reflect findings from SLA research as fully as they could, for commercial and practical reasons (Tomlinson 2012). This is a reason not to reject published materials but to use them critically.

body: Purpose: to show the gap between research and materials. Content: a bridge between a library labelled ‘research’ and a coursebook labelled ‘materials’, with a few planks missing and a teacher placing a new plank. Style: warm. Board version: two boxes joined by a broken line.

items: DIKSHA (free, Government of India) to access state and NCERT textbooks for comparison.

blocks.x: Printed textbook units and a paper checklist.

pts: Research on digital and adaptive materials design continues to develop, connecting to Unit 18's technology principles and the AI discussion closing this tier.
Early evidence suggests genuine benefits alongside real, unresolved questions about engagement and depth of processing.
This remains one of the most actively evolving areas of materials-design research.

v: One digital activity and its paper version

items: Choose a short activity that exists in both forms, for example a vocabulary matching exercise or a reading with questions.
Run the digital version with one group, sharing devices, and the paper version with another group.
Note time on task, completion and one quick measure of learning, such as a five-item check the next day.
Discuss what the digital version added and what it lost. Connect with Unit 18’s technology principles.
Learners try both and say which helped them remember more.
Not applicable (classroom research activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s comparison (written for this book):

lines: Digital group: Very engaged; many guessed quickly until the answer turned green. Next-day check: average 3 of 5.
Paper group: Slower; some discussion in pairs about meanings. Next-day check: average 3.5 of 5.
Note: Small groups, one day. Engagement is not the same as learning. Try adding a ‘say why’ step to the digital task.

blocks.x: Research on digital and adaptive materials is developing quickly. Digital materials can offer immediate feedback, audio and personalization, but open questions remain about whether engagement leads to deeper processing (Mishan and Timmis 2015) [VERIFY chapter on digital materials]. Claims for new tools, including AI-generated materials, deserve the same scrutiny as any other.

body: Purpose: to compare digital and paper activities. Content: one group of learners around a shared tablet, another with a printed sheet; both lead to the same word in a thought bubble. Style: realistic, Indian government school. Board version: a rectangle screen and a sheet of paper, with arrows to one word.

items: Quizlet (free basic plan) or LearningApps.org (free) for simple digital matching tasks.

blocks.x: The same activity as printed cards or a board-drawn matching task.

pts: This research doesn't replace the practical materials-writing judgement built in Tier III — it grounds and refines it.
Periodically checking materials-design choices against current research findings is itself an application of Unit 67's action-research habit.
This closes the loop between this series' practical craft and its underlying scholarly foundation.

v: 20 minutes per material, over a term

items: For one material you write this term, list three design decisions, for example the choice of text, the task type and the amount of planning time.
Beside each, write the research principle it relies on, from this unit or earlier ones.
Use the material, then note what happened: what worked, what did not and what learners said.
Revise the material and record the reason. This follows Unit 67’s action-research cycle.
A group of teachers in a cluster keeps a shared log for a bank of district materials.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A log entry (written for this book):

lines: Decision: Use a local news story about a lake clean-up in Bengaluru. Principle: affective engagement; local relevance.
Decision: Two minutes of planning before the discussion. Principle: planning time supports more complex language.
What happened: Strong interest; discussion slipped into Kannada when opinions got strong.
Revision: Add a short phrase bank for giving opinions; allow Kannada for planning, English for reporting.

blocks.x: The log does not replace judgement; it makes judgement visible and testable. It links the craft of Unit 69 with the evidence in this unit and prepares for Unit 81 on reading research critically.

body: Purpose: to show design as a cycle linking craft and research. Content: a cycle of ‘decide’, ‘link to research’, ‘teach’, ‘observe’ and ‘revise’, with a notebook and a coursebook at the centre. Style: calm. Board version: a circle with five labels.

items: Google Docs (free) or Microsoft OneNote (free) for a shared digital log.

blocks.x: A paper notebook with one page per material.

body: Take one worksheet you used this month. Write down the reason for each of its activities. For any activity where you cannot name a reason, decide whether to keep it, change it or drop it.

dek: Unit 80 of 100: the research base behind grading, authenticity and task design — grounding Tier III's practical materials-writing craft in its underlying evidence.

aims.x: In Unit 69 you wrote your own materials, and the emphasis was on craft: choosing a text, sequencing tasks, writing clear rubrics. This unit asks a different question: what evidence justifies those choices? It examines the research base behind text selection, authenticity, task design and materials evaluation, and it looks honestly at where that evidence is strong, where it is mixed and where it is still developing. The activities suit teachers, materials writers and teacher educators, including DIET faculty who prepare supplementary materials or review textbooks.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe the Text-Driven Approach and contrast it with a language-point-driven approach to materials design;
relate principles of materials development to findings from second language acquisition research;
explain why authenticity is a contested concept and why its benefits should not be assumed;
identify task features, such as information gap, complexity and planning time, that research links to learner performance;
apply an explicit, criterion-referenced framework to evaluate a coursebook unit;
explain why published materials may lag behind research, and use them critically;
weigh the claimed benefits and open questions of digital and adaptive materials;
test a materials-design decision in your own classroom through a small cycle of action research.

why: Why this matters. Materials writing (Tier III, Unit 69) was framed as a craft. This poster examines the research evidence that actually justifies its principles.

background.x: For much of the history of ELT, materials were written from experience and convention: writers produced what had worked before, and publishers produced what sold. From the 1990s, materials development became a field of study in its own right, with its own conferences, journals and research (Tomlinson 2012). Tomlinson (2011) argued that materials should be informed by what second language acquisition (SLA) research suggests about how languages are learned, while accepting that this research rarely offers simple instructions. His principles include rich and recycled exposure to language in use, affective and cognitive engagement, attention to form within meaningful use, and opportunities to communicate for real purposes.

Evaluation developed alongside design. McGrath (2016) and others offered systematic frameworks for choosing and adapting coursebooks, moving evaluation from impression towards explicit criteria. At the same time, researchers questioned familiar assumptions. Widdowson (1978) distinguished the genuineness of a text, a property of its origin, from the authenticity of a learner’s response to it, and Gilmore (2007) showed that the evidence for authentic materials is more varied than enthusiasts often suggest. Task-based research, meanwhile, examined how specific design features shape learner language (Skehan 1998; Ellis 2003).

These debates matter in India. Most learners meet English first through state and NCERT textbooks, and teachers frequently supplement them with worksheets, readers and digital content. NEP 2020 calls for learning that is experiential, enjoyable and grounded in local contexts (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and NCF 2023 encourages the use of local texts, home languages and varied learning resources (NCERT 2023).

Materials research is uneven: some claims rest on many studies, others on a few small ones, and many on principled argument. It does not replace teacher judgement; it offers questions to ask of any material and a habit of checking choices against evidence (Mishan and Timmis 2015).

items: Text-driven sequence. A lesson built from one engaging text, with stages and a language focus that emerges from the text.
Principled evaluation. A criterion-based evaluation of one coursebook unit, with page evidence for each rating.
Task-feature comparison. A short report on changing one task feature in two classes, with the evidence collected and its limits.
Design decision log. A term’s record of decisions for one self-written material, linked to principles, with revisions.
Do you usually start planning from a text or from a language point? Why?
Which of Tomlinson’s principles do your current materials meet least well?
When has an authentic text failed with your learners, and why?
Which task feature would you most like to test in your own classes?
How do you decide whether to trust a claim made about a new digital tool?
Which design choice in your materials rests more on habit than on evidence?

perm: All sequences, notes, discussions, ratings and log entries are written for this book. Texts used in activities, such as newspaper paragraphs or railway announcements, should be short extracts used for classroom teaching, with the source acknowledged. Recording learners requires school permission and, where required, parental consent. Screenshots of Google Docs, Forms, Sheets, Padlet, Audacity, DIKSHA, Quizlet, LearningApps.org or OneNote require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: The quality of being genuine in origin or use: a text may be authentic because it was written for real communication, and a task may be authentic because it reflects what learners do outside class.
A record of the decisions a teacher makes in writing a material, such as the choice of text and task, linked to principles and revised in the light of classroom evidence.
A property of a text produced for a real audience and purpose, not for learners. Widdowson (1978) distinguished it from authenticity, which depends on how a reader engages with the text.

An approach to materials design that starts from a pre-selected grammar or vocabulary item and builds texts and activities to present it, in contrast to a text-driven approach, which starts from an engaging text and draws language work from it.

The field and practice of producing, evaluating and adapting materials for language learning, informed by research on second language acquisition; it became a recognized area of ELT in the 1990s, led by Brian Tomlinson.

The systematic judgement of the value of learning materials against explicit criteria, before, during or after use; an evaluation framework makes those criteria clear and helps teachers compare coursebooks consistently.
Time given before a task for learners to prepare what they will say or write; research links it to greater fluency and complexity in performance.

The distance between what research findings suggest and what actually happens in classrooms, caused partly by inaccessible publications and partly by research that ignores classroom realities. Practitioner research and partnerships aim to narrow it.

Design characteristics of a task, such as the type of information gap, complexity and planning time, that research links to learner performance in fluency, accuracy and complexity (Skehan 1998; Ellis 2003).
An approach to materials design in which an engaging text is chosen first and the language focus emerges from it, rather than a language point determining the text (Tomlinson 2011).
